source.title: Limits of Transformer Language Models on Learning Algorithmic Compositions
source.authors: Jonathan Thomm; Aleksandar Terzic; G. Karunaratne; Giacomo Camposampiero; B. Schölkopf; Abbas Rahimi

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. The title in the supplied metadata differs slightly from the title in the paper text; the text itself is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies compositional algorithmic tasks and few-shot task performance, but it does not measure induction heads, token-index loss, or the training dynamics described by the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports prompted task-solving outcomes for PEN and PERM, which are related to in-context task learning but do not measure induction behavior or the claim's loss-based in-context-learning measure. Those results are recorded as none-version findings. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The paper studies sample efficiency of compositional algorithmic learning (LLaMA trained from scratch) and prompted task accuracy of GPT-4, Gemini-Pro and o1-preview. It never measures induction heads, previous-token heads, attention patterns, loss by token index, or training-time phase changes. The text does not even mention induction heads. So it neither tests nor uses the claim. 'cites_only' is the closest relation; the record's 'discusses' overstates the link, since the text does not discuss induction heads.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude, from LLaMA trained from scratch, that learning a composition needs more samples than the sum of samples for its sub-tasks (hypothesis H4). They back this with a theoretical bound on gradient-descent data inefficiency. They draw no conclusions about induction heads.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce or test the induction-head methods or measures in the original sources; it evaluates compositional algorithmic tasks and prompted task accuracy.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompt format changes task performance: the authors report higher results with hand-crafted sub-task CoT than with less explicit prompting on some tested tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-4 and Gemini-Pro reach 0% task accuracy on PEN under all prompts. On PERM, GPT-4 reaches at most 42% and Gemini-Pro 9%, with hand-crafted sub-task CoT. o1-preview reaches 70% on PEN with a task description and CoT. Increasing from 8 to 32 shots does not raise task accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Few-shot prompting of frontier LLMs fails to reliably compose algorithmic sub-tasks on pointer-execution tasks; success depends on explicit procedural prompts.

record.problems: The paper's tasks are a limited synthetic benchmark, a limitation the authors acknowledge. It reports no uncertainty estimates for these results; its code-interpreter analysis uses 20 randomly selected answers. These limitations concern the paper's own task experiments, not induction-head evidence.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows included. Other prompt-setting values appear in a flattened Table 1 and were not assigned where the text does not unambiguously associate a value with a model, condition, or metric. Cited results were excluded.

untested.parts: Induction-head formation, composition with previous-token heads, and [A][B]…[A]→[B] copying.
Abrupt formation, loss bump, and timing relative to in-context learning gains.
Whether induction heads carry most token-index in-context learning in large models.
Induction heads across families, sizes, runs or modalities.
Dependence of induction-head formation or in-context learning on data and training setup.
Which heads or mechanisms carry few-shot task learning. The prompting results report task accuracy only and contain no mechanism analysis.
Whether formation consists of several sub-steps or overlapping transitions.

record.verdict_notes: The study has no bearing on any version. The LLaMA training results (Tables C.2–C.12) are compositional sample-efficiency measures and are rightly left out as irrelevant to the claim. The PEN matching operation resembles the attention-based lookup that induction heads perform, but the paper does no mechanistic analysis.

versions.untested_parts: Induction-head formation, composition with previous-token heads, and [A][B] … [A] → [B] copying.
Induction-head timing, abruptness, training-loss bump, and coincidence with a gain in loss-based in-context learning.
Whether induction heads carry most loss-based in-context learning in large transformers.
Induction-head behavior across model families, sizes, runs, architectures, or modalities.
Whether induction-head formation or loss-based in-context learning depends on data and training setup.
Whether other heads or mechanisms mainly carry few-shot task learning instead of induction heads.
Whether induction-head formation consists of multiple sub-steps or overlapping transitions.
